question: Compare list.sort() and sorted() in Python.
answer: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None [S1] [S2]. sorted() returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged [S2] [S6] [S1].

citations.text:
3. Lookup Errors Compared
KeyError is raised when a dictionary key is missing. IndexError is raised when a sequence index is
out of range. AttributeError is raised when an object has no attribute of that name.
The message 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'append' almost always means a variable holds
None instead of a list. The classic cause is writing nums = nums.sort(), because list.sort() sorts in
place and returns None. Use nums.sort() on its own line or sorted(nums) when a new list is
needed.
dict.get(key, default) avoids a KeyError, while collections.defaultdict(list) creates a missing key with
an empty list the first time it is accessed, which makes grouping code shorter.

citations.title: Python Reference Notes
citations.text:
BUILT-IN FUNCTIONS
len(x) returns the number of items in x.
sum(nums) adds the numbers in an iterable.
min(nums) and max(nums) return the smallest and largest items.
sorted(items) returns a new sorted list; list.sort() sorts in place and returns None.
enumerate(items) gives (index, item) pairs.
zip(a, b) pairs items from two iterables and stops at the shortest.
range(stop) generates 0 .. stop-1; range(start, stop, step) supports steps.
isinstance(x, int) tests whether x is an instance of a type.

S4.title: Python Reference Notes
S4.text:
COMMON ERRORS AND THEIR MEANING
SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python, for example a missing colon after if.
IndentationError: the indentation of a block is inconsistent.
NameError: a variable or function name was used before it was defined.
TypeError: an operation was applied to the wrong type, such as "a" + 1.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not, such as int("abc").
KeyError: a dictionary key does not exist.
IndexError: a list index is outside the valid range.
ZeroDivisionError: division or modulo by zero.
FileNotFoundError: the file path does not exist.

S5.title: Python Lecture Notes
S5.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).

S7.title: Python Debugging Playbook
S7.text:
4. Performance Pitfalls
functools.lru_cache(maxsize=128) caches the results of a function for repeated arguments; the
default maxsize is 128 and maxsize=None removes the limit. Arguments must be hashable.
Building a long string with += inside a loop copies the string repeatedly; collect the pieces in a list
and call "".join(parts) once. A membership test with in is a linear scan for a list but an average
constant-time lookup for a set or dict, so convert a list to a set when you test membership many
times.
collections.Counter(words).most_common(3) returns the three most frequent items as (item, count)
pairs. Sorting with sorted(items, key=len) is faster and clearer than writing a comparison function.
